newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian govt under attack on Chechnya concessions.
newsitem.headline: Russian govt under attack on Chechnya concessions.

text.p: Russian communists launched a fierce attack on Sunday on new government concessions to Chechen rebels, calling them treacherous moves which would break up Russia in the same way as the Soviet Union.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who signed the new peace agreement on Saturday, defended President Boris Yeltsin's dramatic decision to withdraw the last Russian troops from the breakaway region after nearly two years of war.

Parliament, however, accepted a communist call for a special debate next Friday on what party leader Gennady Zyuganov denounced as a "treacherous plan" worked out by Yeltsin's close entourage without consulting key ministers or the legislature.

The communist-dominated State Duma lower house has little power to overturn government policy. And liberal deputies have already come out in favour of the deal, which meets virtually every rebel demand except the recognition of full independence.

But it will be an uncomfortable week for Yeltsin. He also faces mounting tension in the former Soviet republic of Belarus, where a political compromise brokered by Chernomyrdin between the president and parliament collapsed at the weekend.

"The events of the last few days, the sharp deterioration of the situation in Belarus, a string of terrorist actions in the North Caucasus and the deepening economic crisis demonstrate the incompetence of the executive," Zyuganov told a news conference.

Yeltsin, 65, who had a quintuple heart bypass operation on November 5, is taking a more active role in politics after leaving hospital on Friday for the government sanatorium at Barvikha near Moscow. Doctors are pleased with his progress and say he will be back in the Kremlin before the end of the year.

Zyuganov, who ran second in July's presidential election on a platform calling for the restoration of some form of Soviet Union, accused Yeltsin's close advisers, notably chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais, of selling out Russia's interests.
"What was signed was agreed with no one," Zyuganov told a news conference, saying he wanted the Justice Ministry to review the constitutional legality of the agreement.

"It was discussed nowhere expect perhaps in the close entourage of Mr Yeltsin, which has long failed to take account of Russia's interests and is pursuing the territorial destruction of our country," he said.

Zyuganov also took aim at Chernomyrdin, who has played a high-profile role in Yeltsin's absence was especially notable in recent dealings with the Chechens and in all-night talks in Minsk on Friday, seeking to soothe the alarming Belarus crisis.
Chernomyrdin retorted, in an interview with Itar-Tass news agency, that Zyuganov was ill-informed.

And he defended his efforts in Belarus, blaming Belarus legislators for sinking the compromise but also saying pro-Russian President Alexander Lukashenko, who is seeking new powers in a referendum on Sunday, should have done more to implement the accord.

Zyuganov said the Chechen accord, which lays down relations between Moscow and Chechnya in the run-up to Chechen elections on Janauary 27, was "a malignant tumour, the spread of which will affect the whole organism of the Russian state".
He told Interfax it "smells of a Belovezh Mark 2", referring to the 1991 agreement which formally broke up the Soviet Union.
The deal will be popular with many Russians, though.
Liberal Duma deputy Sergei Yushenkov said the final removal of the troops Yeltsin first sent to crush the Chechen separatists in December 1994 was "a victory for common sense".
An officer in one of the remaining brigades stationed in Grozny told NTV television: "Of course it's good for us. We've been here since the start of the war. The men are tired."
NTV television said the Chechen debacle followed failed intervention elsewhere in the old Soviet Union, like Nagorno-Karabakh, Abkhazia and Moldova's Dnestr district.
"So far, not once have tanks or soldiers been able to stop separatism," the commercial channel's anchorman said. "Every war has ended with talks about some sort of co-existence."
